title: What to Do If Your Bank Account Is Hacked: 8 Steps to Take
excerpt: Learn what to do if your bank account is hacked, including how to stop unauthorized transfers, protect your identity, and secure your money.

content:
## What to Do If Your Bank Account Is Hacked

If you spot an unfamiliar transfer, login alert, or new payee, act quickly. Knowing **what to do if your bank account is hacked** can limit the damage, preserve your rights, and help your bank investigate while the details are still fresh.

Do not wait to see whether the transaction reverses itself. Secure the account first, document what happened, and contact your bank through a number you know is legitimate. The steps below work whether you see one suspicious charge or believe someone has taken over the account.

## 1. Contact your bank immediately

Call the number on the back of your debit card, use the bank's official app, or visit a branch. Do not use a phone number in an unexpected text, email, pop-up, or search ad. Scammers often pose as a bank's fraud department to collect a one-time passcode or persuade you to approve a transfer.

Tell the bank exactly what you noticed:

- The date, amount, and recipient of each transaction you do not recognize
- Any login alerts, password reset emails, or profile changes
- Whether your debit card, phone, or email account may be missing or compromised
- The last transaction you know you made yourself

Ask the representative to secure the account, stop pending transfers where possible, and open a fraud claim. Write down the case number, the representative's name, and the time of the call.

## 2. Lock access and change your credentials

Once you have reached the bank, change the account password from a device you trust. Use a new, unique password that is long enough to be hard to guess. Do not simply add a number to your old password. If you reused that password anywhere else, change those accounts too, starting with your email.

Your email deserves special attention because it can be used to reset financial passwords. Review its recent sign-ins, recovery email, recovery phone, and forwarding rules. Remove anything you did not set up.

Turn on two-factor authentication for your bank and email if it is available. An authenticator app is often more resistant to text-message interception than SMS, but use the strongest option your bank offers. Read [what two-factor authentication is and how it protects financial accounts](/blog/what-is-two-factor-authentication-protect-financial-accounts) for a practical setup guide.

## 3. Freeze or replace compromised cards

If a debit card may be involved, use the bank app to lock it while you speak with the bank. Ask whether a replacement card and account number are necessary. A card lock is helpful, but it does not replace the bank's fraud process.

If your checking account number itself was exposed, the bank may recommend closing the account and opening a new one. That creates some short-term work, but it can be safer than leaving a compromised account open. Before closing it, ask how pending deposits, automatic payments, and disputed transactions will be handled.

## 4. Review every recent transaction and account setting

Look beyond the transaction that first caught your attention. Check checking, savings, credit card, and payment app activity for at least the last 60 days. Review scheduled transfers, linked external accounts, bill pay recipients, Zelle or other payment contacts, mailing address, phone number, email address, and alerts.

Criminals sometimes make a small test transaction before attempting a larger transfer. They may also add a new recipient or change an alert setting so they can act later. Take screenshots or download statements before changes make the evidence harder to find.

For help recognizing a related threat, see [how to spot bank impersonation scams](/blog/how-to-spot-bank-impersonation-scams).

## 5. Dispute unauthorized electronic transfers in writing

Your bank can explain its exact process, but follow up in writing if it asks you to. Keep copies of forms, messages, screenshots, and your fraud case number. Under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act, timing matters for many consumer debit and electronic transfer errors. Reporting promptly gives you the best chance of limiting liability and recovering funds.

Describe only what you know. Avoid guessing how the attacker got in or accepting blame for a transfer you did not authorize. If the bank denies a claim and you disagree, ask for the reason in writing and request the documents or information used in its decision.

## 6. Secure the device and connection you use for banking

A stolen password is not the only way an account can be compromised. Malware, a fake banking app, browser extensions, public Wi-Fi, and an unlocked phone can all create risk.

Start with these checks:

- Install operating system, browser, and banking-app updates
- Run a reputable security scan on the device used to access the account
- Remove browser extensions and apps you do not recognize
- Sign out of old devices and revoke remembered sessions where possible
- Set a strong screen lock and enable remote-wipe features on your phone

Avoid logging in to the bank from a public computer or an unfamiliar Wi-Fi network until you have resolved the issue. If you used a device you do not trust, change your password later from a clean device.

## 7. Protect your credit and identity

An account takeover can be part of a wider identity theft attempt. Check your credit reports for unfamiliar accounts, addresses, and inquiries. You can request free reports through [AnnualCreditReport.com](https://www.annualcreditreport.com/), the federally authorized site.

A credit freeze can make it harder for someone to open new credit in your name. It is free to place and lift with the three major credit bureaus. A fraud alert is another option, although it offers a different level of protection. Our comparison of [a credit freeze versus a credit lock](/blog/credit-freeze-vs-credit-lock) explains the tradeoffs.

If you believe your identity was used, create a recovery plan at [IdentityTheft.gov](https://www.identitytheft.gov/). The site can help you document the incident and identify the next steps for your situation.

## 8. Watch the account after the immediate crisis

Fraud can return through a saved payee, an old card number, or an email account that was never fully secured. For the next several weeks, review your transactions frequently and keep instant alerts turned on for purchases, transfers, password changes, and new recipients.

Update direct deposits and automatic payments carefully if you receive a new account number. Make a simple list of recurring bills, then confirm each change directly with the company. This reduces the chance of missed rent, insurance, or utility payments while you are focused on the fraud claim.

## How to tell a real bank alert from a scam

A real fraud alert can look unsettling, which is why scammers copy them. Pause before clicking anything. A legitimate bank may ask you to confirm activity, but it should not pressure you to move money to a so-called safe account or ask for your full password.

Treat these as warning signs:

- Urgent language that demands action in minutes
- A request for a one-time security code
- Instructions to transfer money to protect it
- A link that does not clearly use your bank's official domain
- A caller who becomes angry when you say you will call back through the number on your card

Hang up and use the official number. That one habit can prevent a scammer from turning a suspicious alert into a real loss.

## What not to do after a bank account hack

Do not delete emails or text messages until you have saved screenshots. Do not keep testing an unfamiliar link to see whether it is real. Do not send a passcode to anyone who contacts you unexpectedly, even if caller ID appears to show your bank. And do not wait for a monthly statement. Banks can often do more when they hear from you quickly.

It is also wise to avoid moving money around randomly before you speak with the bank. Unplanned transfers can make the timeline harder to understand and may leave you short for bills. Follow the bank's instructions, document each action, and keep your own record.

## Build a safer banking routine going forward

Account security is easier when it becomes routine. Use a password manager to create unique passwords, turn on multi-factor authentication, and set transaction alerts at a low threshold. Review linked accounts and payment recipients a few times each year.

You can also use a budget to notice unusual activity faster. When you regularly track your spending, a transaction that does not fit your plan stands out. Pennywise can help you see your normal expenses in one place, so a surprise charge is easier to spot and investigate.

## Frequently asked questions

### Will my bank refund money if my account was hacked?

It depends on the facts, the type of transaction, and how quickly you report it. Contact your bank immediately, submit its fraud claim, and keep records of every conversation and document.

### How long does a bank fraud investigation take?

Timelines vary by bank and transaction type. Ask for a case number, the expected review timeline, and whether provisional credit may be available while the bank investigates.

### Should I close my bank account after it is hacked?

Not always. Your bank may be able to secure the account and replace cards. If the account number, credentials, or personal details were broadly exposed, closing it and opening a new account may be the safer choice.

### Can someone hack my bank account with just my phone number?

A phone number alone is usually not enough, but it can help an attacker attempt a phishing scam or a SIM-swap attack. Protect your phone account with a carrier PIN and never share bank security codes.

## The bottom line

A hacked bank account is stressful, but a calm sequence makes a meaningful difference: contact the bank through an official channel, secure access, document the fraud, and protect your identity. Then keep alerts on and review your accounts regularly. Fast reporting and clear records give you the strongest position while your bank investigates.
